source.title: Structuring Sparsity: Block-Sparse Featurizers Capture Visual Concept Manifolds
source.authors: Thomas Fel; M. Kowal; Mozes Jacobs; Dron Hazra; Usha Bhalla; Lee Sharkey; Lucius Bushnaq; Satchel Grant; Tal Haklay; Thomas Icard; Can Rager; Michael T. Pearce; Daniel Wurgaft; Aiden Swann; Fenil R. Doshi; S. Boppana; Curt Tigges; Nick Cammarata; Thomas Serre; V. Shyam; Owen Lewis; Tom McGrath; Jack Merullo; E. Lubana; Atticus Geiger

record.tranche_reason: The paper reexamines InceptionV1 curve detectors and argues, with its own results, that a population of neurons and directional SAE features gives a fragmented view of a continuous curve manifold. This refines how such features should be interpreted, but does not test the essay’s cat-and-car/pose example.
record.gate_note: The paper’s own InceptionV1 curve analysis bears on V3. Its DINOv3 geometry and description-length measurements concern the choice of feature unit but do not test any listed version’s specific claim; they are recorded under fits_no_version. Cited results from earlier work are not recorded as study results. Values used only for protocol or parameter choices are omitted.
record.test_reason: The InceptionV1 analysis covers curve-detector neurons, which are not a classic polysemantic example. It reports no rate of polysemanticity and makes no superposition-versus-shared-feature argument about any polysemantic neuron, cat-and-car included. Its point is that orientation-tuned neurons and SAE atoms each tile one curve manifold. That bears on whether single neurons or directions are the right unit, a related construct no version names. The DINOv3 and SDXL results concern featurizer design. No version's claim is tested, so the findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. Add that the authors find block sparsity matches a sum-of-manifolds model and gives shorter MDL descriptions than SAEs on DINOv3, with concepts about 2–4 dimensional. They also read 180°-wrapping curve neurons as reading the manifold's second harmonic, and say blocks are not proposed as a universal atom, possibly mismatched for language.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses block-sparse featurizers and manifold/Fourier analysis of vision-model activations, rather than audits of neuron poles or language-model explanation scoring.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported DINOv3 description-length optimum varies by featurizer and dictionary width; the authors describe the minima as shallow and read the direction of the effect rather than a single optimal block size.

fits_no_version.finding: InceptionV1 curve neurons each fire for a narrow orientation wedge and tile 0–360° coarsely. A single Grassmannian BSF block covers all orientations as one connected manifold.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Individually interpretable vision neurons can be fragments of a single population-level manifold feature, so a neuron's 'one job' may be a slice of a continuous variable.

fits_no_version.finding: The curve manifold carries higher Fourier modes: 59/18/12% of variance for the first three modes, well above a matched null. The authors say neurons wrapping at 180° read the second harmonic.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some neuron tuning quirks, such as 180° wrapping, are readouts of higher-order structure in a shared manifold.

fits_no_version.finding: DINOv3 BSF blocks have mean stable rank of 2–4 even when given 16 dimensions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Visual-model concepts are often multi-dimensional rather than single directions.

fits_no_version.finding: Block codes with b>1 have shorter description length than the b=1 SAE across widths and sparsities.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For DINOv3 activations, block-structured features compress better than directional features.

record.problems: The InceptionV1 evidence concerns one curve-orientation analysis and does not test the cat-and-car/pose example or the essay’s recursive-generalization account. The paper does not measure neuron-pole job shares or test explanations on held-out activating examples. Several interpretation results are qualitative.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were left out. Other experiments on toy manifold recovery, DINOv3 concept detection and smoothness, lighting/shadow, and SDXL steering do not measure any listed claim version.

untested.parts: Shares in other language models, dense or mixture-of-experts, at scale (all).
Polysemantic neurons such as cat-and-car, the shared pose feature, and recursive generalization versus superposition (all). Only monosemantic curve detectors are studied.
Interpretable-neuron share as a function of tools, architecture or regularization (all).
Neuron-based attribution graphs versus replacement models (all).
Prediction of firing from activating-example explanations (all).

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked R1–R6 to V3, but curve detectors are monosemantic textbook examples, and the paper makes no claim about polysemantic neurons, superposition, or the cat-and-car case. Its argument that neurons tile a manifold is, if anything, orthogonal to the essay's framing. The study does not cite the essay. Relation is set to discusses or T6 rather than tests.

versions.untested_parts: Qwen3-32B pole shares and independent tests on held-out activations.
Language models, dense and mixture-of-experts models, and scaling to trillions of parameters.
The cat-and-car example, pose as its shared feature, and the essay’s proposed recursive-generalization mechanism.
Shares of interpretable neurons, late-layer causes, architecture or regularization effects on those shares, and the InceptionV1-sized model estimates.
Attribution graphs, explaining model behaviour with its own neurons, and comparison to trained replacement models or reconstruction error.
Whether explanations based on activating examples predict new activation cases.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations on new text.

rows.subject: InceptionV1
rows.operation_detail: Examined neuron tuning to synthetic curves swept over orientation.

conditions.value: synthetic curves with orientation swept from 0° to 360°

rows.value: Individual neurons fire for a narrow wedge of orientations; the original neurons cover orientation coarsely, leaving gaps.
rows.note: The result is about a population of curve-detector neurons and curve orientation, not the cat-and-car/pose example.
rows.check: Curve-detector neurons are not polysemantic. The row measures orientation tiling by a neuron population, not whether a polysemantic neuron has a shared feature. V3 does not apply.

rows.subject: InceptionV1
rows.operation_detail: Compared Top-k SAE atom tuning to synthetic curves swept over orientation.

conditions.value: synthetic curves with orientation swept from 0° to 360°

rows.measure: Orientation coverage and fragmentation of curve responses
rows.value: SAE atoms fill most of the orientation gaps but still shatter the manifold, using a separate atom for each orientation slice.
rows.note: The paper presents the SAE fragmentation as a featurizer artifact, not a property of the network.
rows.check: This compares Top-k SAE atoms with neurons and the BSF, a featurizer comparison rather than a test of V3.

rows.subject: InceptionV1
rows.operation_detail: Measured a Grassmannian BSF block’s response across synthetic curve orientations.

conditions.value: synthetic curves with orientation swept over a full cycle

rows.measure: Continuity and orientation coverage of the recovered curve representation
rows.value: A single block stays active across all orientations and reconstructs the curve manifold as one connected region.
rows.note: The recovered continuous feature is a curve-orientation manifold, not a tested shared pose feature.
rows.check: This is the study's own method (BSF block) result. It shows the method recovers a connected manifold, which does not bear on V3.

rows.subject: InceptionV1
rows.operation_detail: Decomposed a recovered curve block’s contribution into Fourier harmonics as orientation varied.
rows.measure: Share of curve-manifold variance in Fourier modes
rows.value: The first three modes account for 89% of variance (59/18/12%); modes beyond the third share the remaining 11%.
rows.note: The authors interpret the modes as orientation, orientation modulo 180°, and orientation modulo 120°.
rows.check: This is the Fourier decomposition of the BSF block's curve manifold. It is the study's own method output, not a measure of neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: InceptionV1
rows.operation_detail: Passed a pure first-harmonic orientation input through the same trained curve block and Fourier probe.
rows.measure: Percentage of AC variance in Fourier modes k=2 and k=3
rows.note: This is a null condition for the higher-harmonic result.
rows.check: This is a null control for R4 (method validation), not a result on any version.

rows.subject: InceptionV1
rows.operation_detail: Passed first-harmonic orientation plus matched white-in-orientation noise through the same trained curve block and Fourier probe.

conditions.value: orientation plus matched noise carrying 56% of input variance

rows.measure: Percentage of AC variance in Fourier modes k=2 and k=3
rows.note: The control leaves the higher modes at the stated white-noise floor.
rows.check: This is a null control for R4 (method validation), not a result on any version.

rows.subject: DINOv3
rows.operation_detail: Measured stable rank of per-block codes across block dimensions and BSF variants.

conditions.value: Vanilla, Grassmannian, and Group Lasso BSFs

rows.measure: Mean stable rank of per-block code
rows.value: Average stable rank settles between two and four across featurizers, even when blocks are allotted up to 16 dimensions.
rows.locator: Sections 3.4 and Appendix C.4; Figures 8 and 22
rows.note: This measures block dimensionality, not the share of neuron poles with one or more jobs.
rows.check: The linking to none is correct: stable rank of BSF blocks in DINOv3 is not neuron-pole shares.

rows.subject: DINOv3
rows.operation_detail: Compared description length of Grassmannian BSF codes with the b=1 directional SAE.

conditions.value: all widths and sparsities shown in Figure 7

rows.value: Blocks with b>1 describe activations in fewer bits than the b=1 SAE across every width and sparsity; the minimum is at b between 2 and 4.
rows.note: The measure compares featurizer compression, not neuron-pole interpretability.
rows.check: The linking to none is correct: this is an MDL comparison between featurizers.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The paper finds a connected curve manifold in one BSF block, while neurons cover orientations coarsely and SAE atoms fragment the representation; this result concerns curve orientation and a population, not the cat-and-car/pose example (R1–R6).
